questions.q: How does Aliche want you to think about a budget?
a: As a payment to your future self, not a restriction
As a temporary fix until your income rises
As a record of what you have already spent
As a set of rules imposed by your bank
questions.why: The first lesson says money you set aside is what later pays for a holiday or something you never could afford.

questions.q: Which accounts does Aliche suggest you set up?
a: Two checking accounts and two savings accounts
One checking account and one investment account
Three credit cards and one savings account
A single account used for everything
questions.why: The first lesson splits cash from bills and emergencies from long-term goals, ideally with automatic transfers.

questions.q: What is the snowball method of getting out of debt?
a: Paying off debts from smallest to largest
Paying the highest interest debt first
Combining every debt into one new loan
Paying only the minimum on each debt
questions.why: The second lesson contrasts the snowball with the avalanche method, which targets the highest interest rate.

questions.q: What credit utilization does the summary say you should aim for?
a: No more than 30%
No more than 10%
No more than 50%
No more than 75%
questions.why: The second lesson says staying at or below 30% builds credit history without creating a heavy burden.

questions.q: How does Aliche suggest building wealth for retirement?
a: Automate contributions and diversify across stocks and bonds
Keep all your savings in a checking account
Pick one promising stock and hold it
Withdraw your earnings at the end of each month
questions.why: The third lesson recommends steady automated investing and spreading risk rather than chasing single bets.
